blocks.cap: Factor \(3204\) into primes and the pairs are visible, \(3204=2\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot 3\cdot 89\). Each pair leaves the radical as a single copy, the \(2\)s as one \(2\) and the \(3\)s as one \(3\), while the unpaired \(89\) stays inside. Out front \(2\cdot 3=6\), so \(\sqrt{3204}=6\sqrt{89}\).

blocks.x: Two pairs of the same prime this time. \(4941=3^{4}\cdot 61\). Pair the primes to simplify \(\sqrt{4941}\) to \(a\sqrt{b}\) with \(b\) as small as possible. Enter \(a\).
hints: \(3^{4}\) is two separate pairs of \(3\), and each pair leaves the radical as one copy.
The two exited \(3\)s multiply together out front. Only the \(61\) stays inside.
blocks.sol: \(3^{4}=3^{2}\cdot 3^{2}\) is two pairs, and each pair leaves the radical as a \(3\), so \(\sqrt{4941}=3\cdot 3\cdot\sqrt{61}=\boxed{9}\sqrt{61}\). One pair at a time also works, \(\sqrt{4941}=3\sqrt{549}\) and \(549=9\cdot 61\), it just takes two steps.

blocks.x: Not every radical can be simplified. Of \(\sqrt{66}\), \(\sqrt{85}\), \(\sqrt{110}\), and \(\sqrt{348}\), how many can be? Enter the count.
hints: A radical simplifies exactly when some prime repeats in the radicand's factorization.
Factor each radicand and look for a repeated prime. Three of the four have none.
blocks.sol: \(66=2\cdot 3\cdot 11\), \(85=5\cdot 17\), and \(110=2\cdot 5\cdot 11\) have no repeated prime, so those three are already simplified. Only \(348=2^{2}\cdot 3\cdot 29\) has a pair, giving \(2\sqrt{87}\), so the count is \(\boxed{1}\). A squarefree radicand is not stuck, it is finished.

blocks.x: The quotient rule. Division splits the same way. Power of a quotient from 3.1 gives each base its own exponent, so \(\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)^{1/2}=\frac{a^{1/2}}{b^{1/2}}\), which in radical notation is $$\sqrt{\frac{a}{b}}=\frac{\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{b}}$$ for nonnegative \(a\) and positive \(b\). The move that pays is to reduce the fraction under the radical before rooting anything. A fraction that looks hopeless often reduces to a perfect square over a perfect square, and then the root is a plain fraction with no radical left anywhere.
Evaluate \(\sqrt{\dfrac{490}{810}}\) exactly, reducing the fraction under the radical first. Enter the value as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Simplify the fraction before touching the radical.
Divide the top and the bottom by \(10\). Both results are perfect squares.
blocks.sol: \(\frac{490}{810}=\frac{49}{81}\), so $$\sqrt{\frac{490}{810}}=\sqrt{\frac{49}{81}}=\frac{\sqrt{49}}{\sqrt{81}}=\boxed{\frac{7}{9}}.$$ Rooting first leaves \(\sqrt{490}\) over \(\sqrt{810}\), and neither is a whole number. Reducing first made both perfect squares.

blocks.x: Combine \(\sqrt{53}\cdot\sqrt{212}\) under one radical. Neither factor alone is a whole number, but the product is. Enter the whole-number value.
hints: One radical first, then look for pairs among the prime factors.
\(212=4\cdot 53\), so the combined radicand is \(4\cdot 53^{2}\).
blocks.sol: \(\sqrt{53}\cdot\sqrt{212}=\sqrt{53\cdot 212}=\sqrt{4\cdot 53^{2}}=2\cdot 53=\boxed{106}\). Two numbers with no exact decimal form multiplied to a plain whole number, which is why exact forms are worth keeping until the end.

blocks.x: Like radicals. Addition obeys a stricter rule. The like-terms idea from 2.4 transfers whole, \(a\sqrt{b}+c\sqrt{b}=(a+c)\sqrt{b}\) by the distributive property, exactly as \(2x+3x=5x\). But the product rule has no addition twin. \(\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}\) is not \(\sqrt{a+b}\), and radicals only combine under addition when they are like, meaning the same radicand after simplifying. That last clause is the working rule. Unsimplified radicals hide their likeness, so simplify every term first, then compare radicands.
\(\sqrt{204}+\sqrt{459}\) looks like a sum of unlike radicals. Simplify each term, then enter the coefficient of \(\sqrt{51}\) in the sum.
hints: Neither term is simplified yet, and likeness only shows after both are.
blocks.sol: \(\sqrt{204}=2\sqrt{51}\) and \(\sqrt{459}=3\sqrt{51}\), so the sum is \(2\sqrt{51}+3\sqrt{51}=\boxed{5}\sqrt{51}\). The two radicals were like all along. Simplifying is what made it visible.

blocks.x: Compute \(\sqrt{2303}-\sqrt{752}-\sqrt{423}\) exactly. No decimals and no estimating. The exact value is a number you can type. Enter it.
hints: Three ugly radicals can all be multiples of one small radical. Simplify each term first.
Each radicand is a perfect square times \(47\).
blocks.sol: \(2303=49\cdot 47\), \(752=16\cdot 47\), and \(423=9\cdot 47\), so the expression is \(7\sqrt{47}-4\sqrt{47}-3\sqrt{47}=(7-4-3)\sqrt{47}=\boxed{0}\). The surprise is the point. Simplifying can collapse a whole expression to nothing.

blocks.x: Radicals under the old laws. A radical is a fractional power, so every 3.3 move still applies. Powers of radicals collapse through power of a power, \((\sqrt{a})^{4}=(a^{1/2})^{4}=a^{2}\). Cube roots simplify by the same pairing idea, except a prime needs three copies to leave, since \(\sqrt[3]{p\cdot p\cdot p}=p\), so hunt for triples instead of pairs. Letter bases work too. For positive \(y\), \(\sqrt{y^{10}}=\left(y^{10}\right)^{1/2}=y^{5}\), power of a power again, halving the exponent.
A cube root to close. \(344=2^{3}\cdot 43\). Simplify \(\sqrt[3]{344}\) to \(a\sqrt[3]{b}\) with \(b\) as small as possible. Enter \(b\).
hints: Under a cube root a prime needs three copies to leave, not two.
The triple of \(2\)s leaves as a single \(2\). Count what has no triple.
blocks.sol: The triple of \(2\)s leaves the radical as one \(2\), so \(\sqrt[3]{344}=2\sqrt[3]{43}\) and \(b=\boxed{43}\). Pulling out a mere pair of \(2\)s is the square-root habit misfiring, since \(4\) is not a perfect cube.

blocks.x: The radical sign first appeared in print in 1525, in Christoff Rudolff's algebra book Die Coss, as a bare hook with no bar, likely a hurried letter r for radix, Latin for root. The overbar across the radicand came later. Descartes fused the two into today's symbol in 1637.

Look at what this lesson actually did. Radicals were multiplied, split apart, and added when like. Every division came out clean, because every fraction under a radical reduced to perfect squares. 3.5 faces the division that does not come out clean. Its first answers are correct but awkward to work with, and they get a cleanup rule of their own.

review.x: Evaluate \(\sqrt{4900}\).
hints: A bare radical with no index is the square root. You want the number whose square is \(4900\).
\(4900=49\cdot 100\), and both factors are perfect squares.
review.sol: \(4900=49\cdot 100\), so \(\sqrt{4900}=\sqrt{49}\,\sqrt{100}=7\cdot 10=\boxed{70}\). The product rule turns one big square root into two easy ones.

review.x: Enter the exact value of \((\sqrt{83})^{2}\).
hints: You do not need a decimal for \(\sqrt{83}\), and no decimal would be exact anyway. Use what the symbol means.
In exponent form this is \((83^{1/2})^{2}\), a power of a power from 3.1.
review.sol: \(\sqrt{83}\) is the nonnegative number whose square is \(83\), so \((\sqrt{83})^{2}=\boxed{83}\). That is the symbol's whole job. In exponent form, \((83^{1/2})^{2}=83^{1}\) says the same thing.

review.x: Exactly one of \(\sqrt{-512}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{-512}\) names a real number. Enter its value.
hints: Check the index on each radical. The even-root restriction from 3.3 rules one of them out.
What number, multiplied by itself three times, gives \(-512\)?
review.sol: \((-8)^{3}=-512\), so \(\sqrt[3]{-512}=\boxed{-8}\). No real number squares to \(-512\), so \(\sqrt{-512}\) names nothing, while an odd root passes a negative sign straight through.

review.x: A student answers \(-34\) for \(\sqrt{1156}\), and the check \((-34)^{2}=1156\) comes out right. The answer is still wrong. Enter the value of \(\sqrt{1156}\).
hints: The arithmetic in the check is fine. What rules out \(-34\) is the convention on which of the two candidates the symbol names.
\(\sqrt{x}\) is \(x^{1/2}\), so the nonnegative choice from 3.3 applies to the new symbol too.
review.sol: \(34^{2}=1156\), so \(\sqrt{1156}=\boxed{34}\). Both \(34\) and \(-34\) square to \(1156\), and the radical sign names the nonnegative one, the same convention \(1156^{1/2}\) carried in 3.3. The other candidate is written \(-\sqrt{1156}\).

review.x: A student claims that \(\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{a+b}\). Test the claim the 1.4 way at \(a=9\) and \(b=16\), then enter the true value of \(\sqrt{9}+\sqrt{16}\).
hints: Work each side on its own. The claim only stands if the two sides agree.
Evaluate \(\sqrt{9}\) and \(\sqrt{16}\) separately, then compare their sum with \(\sqrt{25}\).
review.sol: \(\sqrt{9}+\sqrt{16}=3+4=\boxed{7}\). The claim would need \(\sqrt{9+16}=\sqrt{25}=5\) to equal \(7\), and it does not. The product rule splits multiplication across a radical, but it has no addition twin.

review.x: Simplify \(\sqrt{152}\) to the form \(a\sqrt{38}\). Enter \(a\).
hints: You are told what stays under the radical, so the only question is which perfect square comes out.
Divide \(152\) by \(38\) to find the perfect-square factor.

review.x: Simplify \(\sqrt{142}\) to \(a\sqrt{b}\) with \(b\) as small as possible. Enter \(b\).
hints: Factor the radicand into primes and look for a repeated prime. Only pairs come out.
\(142=2\cdot 71\). Does any prime appear twice?
review.sol: \(142=2\cdot 71\) has no repeated prime, so nothing comes out. \(\sqrt{142}\) is already \(1\cdot\sqrt{142}\), and \(b=\boxed{142}\). A squarefree radicand means the radical is finished, not that you missed a trick.

review.x: Simplify \(\sqrt{585}\) to \(a\sqrt{b}\) with \(b\) as small as possible. Enter the product \(a\cdot b\), a times b, as a single number.
hints: Find the largest perfect-square factor of \(585\) first, then multiply the two parts of your simplified form.
\(585\) is divisible by \(9\).
review.sol: \(585=9\cdot 65\), so \(\sqrt{585}=3\sqrt{65}\), and \(a\cdot b=3\cdot 65=\boxed{195}\). Since \(65=5\cdot 13\) has no repeated prime, \(b\) is as small as it can get.

review.x: Evaluate \(\sqrt{\dfrac{96}{150}}\) exactly. Enter a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Reduce the fraction under the radical before rooting anything.
Divide top and bottom by \(6\) and both become perfect squares.
review.sol: \(\frac{96}{150}=\frac{16}{25}\), so \(\sqrt{\frac{96}{150}}=\frac{\sqrt{16}}{\sqrt{25}}=\frac{4}{5}\), \(\boxed{4/5}\). Rooting \(96\) and \(150\) separately leaves a mess that the one reduction avoids.

review.x: \(\sqrt{624}-\sqrt{351}\) simplifies all the way down to a single radical \(\sqrt{b}\). Enter \(b\).
hints: Subtracting the radicands is not a legal move. Simplify each radical on its own and see what they share.
review.sol: \(\sqrt{624}=4\sqrt{39}\) and \(\sqrt{351}=3\sqrt{39}\), so the difference is \(4\sqrt{39}-3\sqrt{39}=1\sqrt{39}\) and \(b=\boxed{39}\). Subtracting radicands would give \(\sqrt{273}\), which is wrong, since no rule pushes subtraction under a radical.

review.x: For positive \(y\), \(\sqrt{y^{194}}=y^{k}\). Enter \(k\).
hints: Rewrite the radical as a \(\frac{1}{2}\) power, then use power of a power from 3.1.
The exponents multiply, \(194\cdot\frac{1}{2}\).
review.sol: \(\sqrt{y^{194}}=(y^{194})^{1/2}=y^{194\cdot\frac{1}{2}}=y^{97}\), so \(k=\boxed{97}\). Halving the exponent works whenever the base is positive and the exponent is even.

review.x: Evaluate \((\sqrt{46})^{4}\).
hints: Write the radical as a half power and let power of a power do the work.
review.sol: \((\sqrt{46})^{4}=(46^{1/2})^{4}=46^{2}=\boxed{2116}\). Grouping as \(((\sqrt{46})^{2})^{2}=46^{2}\) says the same thing without exponent notation.

review.x: Combine \(\sqrt{657}\cdot\sqrt{146}\) under one radical, then simplify to \(a\sqrt{b}\) with \(b\) as small as possible. Enter \(a\).
hints: Merge first, then factor the combined radicand into primes and pull out every pair.
\(657=3^{2}\cdot 73\) and \(146=2\cdot 73\), so the product hides two pairs.
review.sol: \(657\cdot 146=3^{2}\cdot 73^{2}\cdot 2\), so \(\sqrt{657}\,\sqrt{146}=3\cdot 73\cdot\sqrt{2}=\boxed{219}\sqrt{2}\). Multiplying out to \(95922\) first also works, but the pairs are easier to see before the multiplication buries them.

review.x: Evaluate \(\sqrt{\dfrac{126}{686}}\) exactly. Enter a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The fraction reduces a long way before any rooting happens.
Top and bottom share a factor of \(14\).
review.sol: \(\frac{126}{686}=\frac{9}{49}\), so the root is \(\frac{\sqrt{9}}{\sqrt{49}}=\frac{3}{7}\), \(\boxed{3/7}\). Neither \(126\) nor \(686\) is a perfect square on its own, and the single reduction is what makes both layers come out clean.

review.x: Simplify \(\sqrt[3]{472}\) to \(a\sqrt[3]{b}\) with \(b\) as small as possible. Enter \(b\).
hints: Under a cube root a prime needs three copies to come out, not two.
review.sol: \(472=2^{3}\cdot 59\), and the triple of \(2\)s exits as one \(2\), so \(\sqrt[3]{472}=2\sqrt[3]{59}\) and \(b=\boxed{59}\). Writing \(2\sqrt[3]{118}\) from \(472=4\cdot 118\) is the square-root habit misfiring, since a pair of \(2\)s does nothing under a cube root.

review.x: Factor \(5056\) into primes to simplify \(\sqrt{5056}\) to \(a\sqrt{b}\) with \(b\) as small as possible. Enter the product \(a\cdot b\), a times b, as a single number.
hints: Keep halving. The factorization is one odd prime under a tall stack of \(2\)s, and every pair of \(2\)s exits.
\(5056=2^{6}\cdot 79\), and \(2^{6}\) is three separate pairs.
review.sol: \(5056=2^{6}\cdot 79\). The three pairs of \(2\)s leave as \(2\cdot 2\cdot 2=8\) and the unpaired \(79\) stays, so \(\sqrt{5056}=8\sqrt{79}\) and \(a\cdot b=8\cdot 79=\boxed{632}\). Stopping early at \(4\sqrt{316}\) or \(2\sqrt{1264}\) leaves a square inside, and \(b\) is only as small as possible once no prime repeats.

review.x: Simplify \(\sqrt{335}\cdot\sqrt{737}\) to \(a\sqrt{b}\) with \(b\) as small as possible. Enter the sum \(a+b\), a plus b, as a single number.
hints: Combine the two under one radical first. Neither radicand hides a square on its own, but the two share a prime.
review.sol: \(335\cdot 737=5\cdot 67\cdot 11\cdot 67=67^{2}\cdot 55\), so \(\sqrt{335}\,\sqrt{737}=67\sqrt{55}\), and \(a+b=67+55=\boxed{122}\). The shared \(67\) is invisible until both radicands sit under one radical, which is why combining comes first.

blocks.x: 3.4 ended by pointing at the division that does not come out clean. Divide \(6\) by \(\sqrt{3}\). One student stops at \(\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}\), another writes \(2\sqrt{3}\). The forms look nothing alike, so test them the 1.4 way. Square each exactly, and both land on the same whole number. Enter it.
hints: Squaring removes each radical exactly, so both forms square to plain numbers you can compare.
Use \(\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{b}}\right)^{2}=\frac{a^{2}}{b}\) on the first form and \((c\sqrt{b})^{2}=c^{2}\cdot b\) on the second.
blocks.sol: \(\left(\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^{2}=\frac{36}{3}=12\) and \((2\sqrt{3})^{2}=4\cdot 3=\boxed{12}\). Two positive numbers with the same square must be equal, so both forms name the same number and both answers to the division are correct. This lesson decides which form counts as finished.

blocks.x: Both forms are right, and they are equal. Fractions had the same problem. \(\frac{69}{92}\) reduces to \(\frac{3}{4}\), one number with two spellings, and lowest terms settled which spelling counts as finished. Radicals need a standard form of their own. Before choosing it, name the kind of number sitting in that denominator.

Rational and irrational numbers. A rational number is one that can be written as a fraction of two integers. Every integer can be, and so can \(\sqrt{225}\), which equals \(15\). The symbol does not decide, the value does. A number equal to no fraction of integers is irrational, and \(\sqrt{3}\) is one. 3.4 already said no whole number or fraction squares to \(3\), and that claim is used here, not proved. For the hook, \(\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}\) keeps its irrational part in the denominator while \(2\sqrt{3}\) keeps it in the numerator. Only where it sits differs.
Of the four numbers \(\sqrt{225}\), \(\sqrt{33}\), \(-\frac{7}{20}\), and \(0.6\), how many are rational? Enter the count.
hints: Test each one against the definition, writable as one integer over another. A radical can hide a whole number.
\(15^{2}=225\). Is \(33\) a perfect square?
blocks.sol: \(\sqrt{225}=15\), \(-\frac{7}{20}\) is already a fraction of integers, and \(0.6=\frac{3}{5}\), while \(33\) is no perfect square, so \(\sqrt{33}\) is irrational and the count is \(\boxed{3}\). Judge each number by its value, not by how it happens to be written.

blocks.x: The standard form. Fractions get reduced to lowest terms so that any two answers can be compared at a glance. The same convention extends to radicals. A finished answer carries no radical in its denominator. Rewriting a fraction so that its denominator becomes rational is called rationalizing the denominator, and it is the cleanup rule 3.4 promised. The value never changes, only how it is written. So \(\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}\) and \(2\sqrt{3}\) are the same number, and \(2\sqrt{3}\) is the one in standard form.

\(\frac{\sqrt{13}}{\sqrt{13}}\) equals \(1\), and multiplying by \(1\) changes nothing. Multiply \(\frac{9}{\sqrt{13}}\) by it, then use the product rule from 3.4 on the bottom. Enter the denominator of the result.
hints: The whole question is what \(\sqrt{13}\cdot\sqrt{13}\) equals.
By the product rule, \(\sqrt{13}\cdot\sqrt{13}=\sqrt{13\cdot 13}=\sqrt{169}\).
blocks.sol: \(\frac{9}{\sqrt{13}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{13}}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{9\sqrt{13}}{\sqrt{169}}=\frac{9\sqrt{13}}{13}\), so the denominator is \(\boxed{13}\). The radical did not vanish, it moved to the numerator, and the denominator became an integer.

blocks.x: Rationalizing \(\frac{a}{\sqrt{b}}\). Since \(\frac{\sqrt{b}}{\sqrt{b}}=1\) and \(\sqrt{b}\cdot\sqrt{b}=b\) by the product rule, $$\frac{a}{\sqrt{b}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{b}}{\sqrt{b}}=\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{b}.$$ The denominator becomes an integer and the numerator absorbs the radical. The move is legal because it is multiplication by \(1\), which never changes a value. From here on, answers go in the form \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction \(\frac{a}{c}\) in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive.
Rationalize \(\frac{4}{\sqrt{11}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive. Enter \(a+b+c\).
hints: Multiply by \(1\) written as \(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{11}}\).
The result is \(\frac{4\sqrt{11}}{11}\). Read off the three numbers.
blocks.sol: \(\frac{4}{\sqrt{11}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{11}}=\frac{4\sqrt{11}}{11}\), so \(a+b+c=4+11+11=\boxed{26}\). Nothing cancels here, since \(4\) and \(11\) share no factor.

blocks.x: Reduce after, simplify before. The move plants \(b\) in the denominator, and the coefficient upstairs may share a factor with it. Cancel that like any fraction, coefficient against denominator, never the radicand against anything. It also pays to work small. Simplify the denominator's radical first, the 3.4 way, or reduce the fraction first. Both roads reach the same standard form, one just carries smaller numbers the whole way.
Rationalize \(\frac{508}{\sqrt{127}}\) and reduce. The result is a whole multiple of the radical, \(a\sqrt{127}\). Enter \(a\).
hints: Rationalizing is not the last step here. A fraction appears, and it reduces.
After the move you have \(\frac{508\sqrt{127}}{127}\). That fraction is not in lowest terms yet.
blocks.sol: \(\frac{508}{\sqrt{127}}=\frac{508\sqrt{127}}{127}=4\sqrt{127}\), since \(508=4\cdot 127\), so \(a=\boxed{4}\). Stopping at \(\frac{508\sqrt{127}}{127}\) is the common miss. That answer is correct but not in lowest terms.

blocks.x: Rationalize \(\frac{10}{\sqrt{15}}\). Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive. Enter \(a+b+c\).
hints: After the move, the plain fraction part is not yet in lowest terms.
\(\gcd(10,15)=5\). Cancel it between the coefficient and the denominator.
blocks.sol: \(\frac{10}{\sqrt{15}}=\frac{10\sqrt{15}}{15}=\frac{2\sqrt{15}}{3}\), so \(a+b+c=2+15+3=\boxed{20}\). The \(5\) cancels between \(10\) and \(15\). The radicand \(15\) stays put, it is not part of the plain fraction.

blocks.x: Simplify the radical first this time, the 3.4 way, then rationalize \(\frac{226}{\sqrt{452}}\). Everything collapses to a single radical \(\sqrt{b}\). Enter \(b\).
hints: \(452\) has a perfect-square factor. Take it out before touching the fraction.
\(\sqrt{452}=2\sqrt{113}\), so the fraction is \(\frac{226}{2\sqrt{113}}=\frac{113}{\sqrt{113}}\).
blocks.sol: \(\sqrt{452}=2\sqrt{113}\), so \(\frac{226}{\sqrt{452}}=\frac{226}{2\sqrt{113}}=\frac{113}{\sqrt{113}}=\frac{113\sqrt{113}}{113}=\sqrt{113}\), and \(b=\boxed{113}\). The brute road \(\frac{226\sqrt{452}}{452}\) lands in the same place, just with uglier numbers along the way.

blocks.x: Denominators like \(m\sqrt{b}\). In \(\frac{a}{m\sqrt{b}}\) only the radical factor is irrational. The integer \(m\) is already fine and stays, so multiply by \(\frac{\sqrt{b}}{\sqrt{b}}\) alone, $$\frac{a}{m\sqrt{b}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{b}}{\sqrt{b}}=\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{mb}.$$ Two wrong turns tempt here. Multiplying by \(\frac{m\sqrt{b}}{m\sqrt{b}}\) still works but inflates every number for no gain, and squaring the \(m\) changes the value of the fraction, which no rewrite is allowed to do.
Rationalize \(\frac{214}{5\sqrt{107}}\) and reduce fully. Write the result as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive. Enter \(a+b+c\).
hints: Multiply the top and bottom by \(\sqrt{107}\). The result is not yet in lowest terms.
That gives \(\frac{214\sqrt{107}}{535}\), and \(535=5\cdot 107\).
blocks.sol: \(\frac{214}{5\sqrt{107}}=\frac{214\sqrt{107}}{5\cdot 107}=\frac{214\sqrt{107}}{535}=\frac{2\sqrt{107}}{5}\), so \(a+b+c=2+107+5=\boxed{114}\). The common factor is easy to miss because it is the radicand itself. \(107\) divides both \(214\) and \(535\).

blocks.x: Square roots of fractions. The quotient rule from 3.4 splits \(\sqrt{\frac{a}{b}}\) into \(\frac{\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{b}}\). Simplify each radical, then rationalize whatever is left in the denominator. One shortcut is worth checking first. Reduce the fraction under the radical before splitting, since the reduced denominator is sometimes a perfect square, and then there is nothing left to rationalize at all.
Write \(\sqrt{\dfrac{19}{27}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive. Here \(a\) may be \(1\). Enter \(a+b+c\).
hints: The fraction is already in lowest terms, so split it with the quotient rule.
\(\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3}\), so the job is to rationalize \(\frac{\sqrt{19}}{3\sqrt{3}}\).
blocks.sol: \(\sqrt{\frac{19}{27}}=\frac{\sqrt{19}}{\sqrt{27}}=\frac{\sqrt{19}}{3\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{19}\cdot\sqrt{3}}{3\cdot 3}=\frac{\sqrt{57}}{9}\), so \(a+b+c=1+57+9=\boxed{67}\). The numerator radicals merged into \(\sqrt{57}\) by the product rule.

blocks.x: Write \(\sqrt{\dfrac{105}{48}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive, reducing the fraction under the radical before anything else. Here \(a\) may be \(1\). Enter \(a+b+c\).
hints: \(105\) and \(48\) share a factor, and the reduced denominator is special.
\(\frac{105}{48}=\frac{35}{16}\), and \(16\) is a perfect square.
blocks.sol: \(\frac{105}{48}=\frac{35}{16}\), so \(\sqrt{\dfrac{105}{48}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{35}{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{35}}{4}\) and \(a+b+c=1+35+4=\boxed{40}\). Reducing first left nothing to rationalize. The denominator came out whole on its own.

blocks.x: Cube-root denominators. One extra copy is not enough, since \(\sqrt[3]{b}\cdot\sqrt[3]{b}=\sqrt[3]{b^{2}}\), still a radical. 3.4 said a prime leaves a cube root only in triples, so supply both missing copies at once. Multiply by \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{b^{2}}}{\sqrt[3]{b^{2}}}\), and the denominator becomes \(\sqrt[3]{b^{3}}=b\), an integer. The idea is unchanged, multiply by \(1\), chosen so the radical underneath completes to a whole power.
Rationalize \(\frac{84}{\sqrt[3]{131}}\), a cube root in the denominator this time. The result has the form \(\frac{84\sqrt[3]{d}}{131}\). Enter \(d\).
hints: How many copies of \(131\) must sit under a cube root before it comes out whole?
You need \(131^{3}\) in the denominator, so multiply by \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{131^{2}}}{\sqrt[3]{131^{2}}}\).
blocks.sol: \(\frac{84}{\sqrt[3]{131}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt[3]{131^{2}}}{\sqrt[3]{131^{2}}}=\frac{84\sqrt[3]{131^{2}}}{\sqrt[3]{131^{3}}}=\frac{84\sqrt[3]{17161}}{131}\), so \(d=131^{2}=\boxed{17161}\). One extra copy would have left \(\sqrt[3]{131^{2}}\) in the denominator, still irrational.

blocks.x: Rational and irrational both come from ratio. The Pythagoreans found that a square's diagonal is no ratio of whole numbers, and Greek writers called such lengths alogos, without ratio. The story that Hippasus drowned for revealing it is legend, not record.

One expression, every tool. Write \(\frac{18}{\sqrt{14}}+2\sqrt{14}\) as a single fraction \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive. Rationalize first, then combine like radicals as in 3.4 over a common denominator as in 2.5. Enter \(a+b+c\).
hints: Rationalize and reduce the first term. Both terms then become multiples of \(\sqrt{14}\).
blocks.sol: \(\frac{18}{\sqrt{14}}=\frac{18\sqrt{14}}{14}=\frac{9\sqrt{14}}{7}\), and \(2\sqrt{14}=\frac{14\sqrt{14}}{7}\), so the sum is \(\frac{9\sqrt{14}+14\sqrt{14}}{7}=\frac{23\sqrt{14}}{7}\) and \(a+b+c=23+14+7=\boxed{44}\). Standard form is what made the two terms combinable at all.

blocks.x: Chapter 3 stretched the exponent laws to zero, negatives, and fractions, turned fractional powers into radicals, and closed with a standard form for answers. All of it was rewriting, one expression traded for an equal one. Chapter 4 turns to solving, where a claim of equality can be true or false. 4.1 starts with what an equation says.

review.x: Exactly one of \(\sqrt{81}\) and \(\sqrt{87}\) is rational. Decide which one, and enter the value of the rational one as a plain integer.
hints: Rational means writable as a fraction of two integers, and the square root of a perfect square is a whole number. Check whether each radicand is a perfect square.
List the perfect squares near \(80\) and \(90\). One of the two radicands is on that list, and the other sits strictly between two consecutive squares.
review.sol: \(81=9^{2}\), so \(\sqrt{81}=\boxed{9}\), which is rational. \(87\) sits between \(9^{2}=81\) and \(10^{2}=100\), so no integer squares to \(87\), and 3.4 said no fraction does either, so \(\sqrt{87}\) is irrational.

review.x: To rationalize a fraction whose denominator is \(\sqrt{95}\), you multiply by \(\frac{\sqrt{95}}{\sqrt{95}}\). Enter the value of that multiplier as a single number.
hints: Any nonzero number divided by itself gives the same result, no matter how complicated the number looks.
That value is the whole reason the move is legal. Multiplying by it cannot change what the fraction is worth.
review.sol: \(\sqrt{95}\) is a nonzero number, and any nonzero number over itself equals \(\boxed{1}\). Multiplying by \(1\) changes how a fraction looks, never its value, and that is what makes rationalizing legal.

review.x: Rationalizing works because of one product. Enter the exact value of \(\sqrt{103}\cdot\sqrt{103}\).
hints: Use what the symbol means. \(\sqrt{103}\) is the nonnegative number whose square is \(103\).
By the product rule, \(\sqrt{103}\cdot\sqrt{103}=\sqrt{103\cdot 103}\).
review.sol: \(\sqrt{103}\cdot\sqrt{103}=\sqrt{103^{2}}=\boxed{103}\). This product is what every rationalization uses. One more copy of the radical turns it into an integer.

review.x: Rationalize \(\frac{12}{\sqrt{89}}\) and write it as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive. Enter \(c\).
hints: The new denominator is whatever \(\sqrt{89}\cdot\sqrt{89}\) equals.
Check for cancellation afterward. \(89\) is prime and does not divide \(12\), so nothing cancels.
review.sol: \(\frac{12}{\sqrt{89}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{89}}{\sqrt{89}}=\frac{12\sqrt{89}}{89}\), already in lowest terms, so \(c=\boxed{89}\).

review.x: Rationalize \(\frac{16}{\sqrt{55}}\) and write it as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive. Enter \(a+b+c\), a plus b plus c, as a single number.
hints: Multiply by \(1\) written as \(\frac{\sqrt{55}}{\sqrt{55}}\), then check whether anything cancels.
Once the denominator is a whole number, confirm the numerator shares no factor with it and the number under the root has no square factor, then add the three values.
review.sol: \(\frac{16}{\sqrt{55}}=\frac{16\sqrt{55}}{55}\). Since \(16\) and \(55\) share no factor, this is finished, and \(a+b+c=16+55+55=\boxed{126}\).

review.x: Rationalizing never changes a number's value, and squaring can prove it. Square \(\frac{50}{\sqrt{8}}\) exactly and enter the result as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: A square removes the radical exactly, so the top and the bottom both become plain integers.
\(\left(\frac{50}{\sqrt{8}}\right)^{2}=\frac{2500}{8}\), which is not yet in lowest terms.
review.sol: \(\left(\frac{50}{\sqrt{8}}\right)^{2}=\frac{50^{2}}{(\sqrt{8})^{2}}=\frac{2500}{8}=\boxed{\frac{625}{2}}\). Rationalized or not, \(\frac{50}{\sqrt{8}}\) squares to this same number, which is what calling the two forms equal means.

review.x: Rationalize \(\frac{60}{\sqrt{30}}\) and reduce. The result is a whole multiple of the radical, \(a\sqrt{30}\). Enter \(a\).
hints: After multiplying by \(\frac{\sqrt{30}}{\sqrt{30}}\), treat the plain fraction like any fraction and reduce it.
\(\sqrt{30}\cdot\sqrt{30}=30\), so the new denominator is 30. Divide 60 by it to find the whole number in front of the radical.
review.sol: \(\frac{60}{\sqrt{30}}=\frac{60\sqrt{30}}{30}=2\sqrt{30}\), so \(a=\boxed{2}\). Stopping at \(\frac{60\sqrt{30}}{30}\) leaves the fraction unreduced, so it is not standard form yet.

review.x: A student rationalizes \(\frac{58}{\sqrt{58}}\) by multiplying only the denominator by \(\sqrt{58}\), gets \(\frac{58}{58}\), and answers \(1\). The real value is \(\sqrt{b}\). Enter \(b\).
hints: Multiplying only the bottom changes the fraction's value. The multiplier has to hit top and bottom together to stay a multiplication by \(1\).
Done correctly, the fraction becomes \(\frac{58\sqrt{58}}{58}\).
review.sol: \(\frac{58}{\sqrt{58}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{58}}{\sqrt{58}}=\frac{58\sqrt{58}}{58}=\sqrt{58}\), so \(b=\boxed{58}\). The student's one-sided move divided the value by \(\sqrt{58}\), which no rewrite is allowed to do.

review.x: Rationalize \(\frac{25}{2\sqrt{139}}\) and write it as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive. Enter \(c\).
hints: Only the radical factor is irrational. The \(2\) is already fine, so multiply by \(\frac{\sqrt{139}}{\sqrt{139}}\) alone.
After multiplying, the denominator is a whole number. Check whether it shares a factor with \(25\) before you read off \(c\).
review.sol: \(\frac{25}{2\sqrt{139}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{139}}{\sqrt{139}}=\frac{25\sqrt{139}}{2\cdot 139}=\frac{25\sqrt{139}}{278}\). Since \(25\) and \(278\) share no factor, \(c=\boxed{278}\).

review.x: Rationalize \(\frac{93}{4\sqrt{62}}\) and reduce fully. Write it as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive. Enter \(a+b+c\), a plus b plus c, as a single number.
hints: Multiply by \(\frac{\sqrt{62}}{\sqrt{62}}\) alone, then hunt for a common factor. There is one, and it is not small.
The move gives \(\frac{93\sqrt{62}}{248}\), and \(31\) divides both \(93\) and \(248\).
review.sol: \(\frac{93}{4\sqrt{62}}=\frac{93\sqrt{62}}{4\cdot 62}=\frac{93\sqrt{62}}{248}\). Both \(93=3\cdot 31\) and \(248=8\cdot 31\) carry a \(31\), so the fraction reduces to \(\frac{3\sqrt{62}}{8}\), and \(a+b+c=3+62+8=\boxed{73}\).

review.x: Write \(\sqrt{\dfrac{21}{40}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive, where \(a\) may be \(1\). Enter \(b+c\), b plus c, as a single number.
hints: The fraction is already in lowest terms, so split it with the quotient rule and simplify the bottom radical before rationalizing.
\(\sqrt{40}=2\sqrt{10}\), and when you rationalize, the radicals upstairs merge by the product rule.
review.sol: \(\sqrt{\frac{21}{40}}=\frac{\sqrt{21}}{\sqrt{40}}=\frac{\sqrt{21}}{2\sqrt{10}}=\frac{\sqrt{21}\cdot\sqrt{10}}{2\cdot 10}=\frac{\sqrt{210}}{20}\), so \(b+c=210+20=\boxed{230}\). Simplifying \(\sqrt{40}\) first kept every number small.

review.x: Write \(\sqrt{\dfrac{258}{75}}\) as \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive, where \(a\) may be \(1\). Reduce the fraction under the radical first. Enter \(b+c\), b plus c, as a single number.
hints: Reducing first can make rationalizing unnecessary. See what \(258\) and \(75\) have in common.
\(\frac{258}{75}=\frac{86}{25}\), and \(25\) is a perfect square.
review.sol: \(\frac{258}{75}=\frac{86}{25}\), so \(\sqrt{\frac{258}{75}}=\frac{\sqrt{86}}{\sqrt{25}}=\frac{\sqrt{86}}{5}\) and \(b+c=86+5=\boxed{91}\). Reducing first left a perfect square downstairs, so there was nothing to rationalize.

review.x: Evaluate \(\sqrt{\dfrac{284}{639}}\) exactly, reducing the fraction under the radical first. Enter your answer as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The fraction hides a large common factor, and what remains after reducing is friendlier than it looks.
\(71\) divides both \(284\) and \(639\), leaving \(\frac{4}{9}\).
review.sol: \(284=4\cdot 71\) and \(639=9\cdot 71\), so \(\frac{284}{639}=\frac{4}{9}\) and \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}}=\frac{\sqrt{4}}{\sqrt{9}}=\boxed{\frac{2}{3}}\). No radical remains, since both parts of the reduced fraction are perfect squares.

review.x: Rationalize the cube-root denominator in \(\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{109}}\). The result has the form \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{n}}{109}\). Enter \(n\).
hints: A prime leaves a cube root only in triples. One copy of \(109\) is present, so count what is missing.
review.sol: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{109}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt[3]{109^{2}}}{\sqrt[3]{109^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt[3]{109^{2}}}{\sqrt[3]{109^{3}}}=\frac{\sqrt[3]{11881}}{109}\), so \(n=\boxed{11881}\). Multiplying by just one more copy would leave \(\sqrt[3]{109^{2}}\) downstairs, still irrational.

review.x: \(22201=149^{2}\), so \(\sqrt[3]{22201}\) already holds two copies of \(149\). To rationalize \(\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{22201}}\), multiply by \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{n}}{\sqrt[3]{n}}\) with \(n\) as small as possible. Enter \(n\).
hints: Count the copies of \(149\) under the cube root and compare with the triple a cube root needs.
Two copies are present, so only one more is missing.
review.sol: \(\sqrt[3]{149^{2}}\cdot\sqrt[3]{149}=\sqrt[3]{149^{3}}=149\), so \(n=\boxed{149}\) and the fraction becomes \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{149}}{149}\). Multiplying by \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{22201^{2}}}{\sqrt[3]{22201^{2}}}\) also works but brings in far bigger numbers for the same answer.

review.x: Compute \(\frac{39}{\sqrt{78}}+\frac{\sqrt{78}}{2}\). Once the first term is in standard form, the sum collapses to a single radical \(\sqrt{n}\). Enter \(n\).
hints: Rationalize and reduce the first term before adding anything. Then 3.4's like radicals take over.
\(\frac{39}{\sqrt{78}}=\frac{39\sqrt{78}}{78}=\frac{\sqrt{78}}{2}\), the same as the second term.
review.sol: \(\frac{39}{\sqrt{78}}=\frac{39\sqrt{78}}{78}=\frac{\sqrt{78}}{2}\), so the sum is \(\frac{\sqrt{78}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{78}}{2}=\frac{2\sqrt{78}}{2}=\sqrt{78}\) and \(n=\boxed{78}\). The two terms were equal all along, and standard form is what made that visible.

review.x: Write \(\frac{47}{\sqrt{94}}+\frac{\sqrt{94}}{4}\) as one fraction \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive. Enter \(a+b+c\), a plus b plus c, as a single number.
hints: Rationalize and reduce the first term, then put both terms over a common denominator the 2.5 way.
review.sol: \(\frac{47}{\sqrt{94}}=\frac{47\sqrt{94}}{94}=\frac{\sqrt{94}}{2}=\frac{2\sqrt{94}}{4}\), so the sum is \(\frac{2\sqrt{94}}{4}+\frac{\sqrt{94}}{4}=\frac{3\sqrt{94}}{4}\) and \(a+b+c=3+94+4=\boxed{101}\). Neither term could combine with the other until the radical left the denominator.

review.x: Write \(\frac{201}{\sqrt{134}}-\sqrt{134}\) as one fraction \(\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}\) with \(b\) squarefree, the fraction in lowest terms, and \(c\) positive, where \(a\) may be \(1\). Enter \(b+c\), b plus c, as a single number.
hints: Rationalize and reduce the first term before subtracting, then write \(\sqrt{134}\) over the same denominator.
review.sol: \(\frac{201}{\sqrt{134}}=\frac{201\sqrt{134}}{134}=\frac{3\sqrt{134}}{2}\), and \(\sqrt{134}=\frac{2\sqrt{134}}{2}\), so the difference is \(\frac{3\sqrt{134}}{2}-\frac{2\sqrt{134}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{134}}{2}\) and \(b+c=134+2=\boxed{136}\). The whole coefficient collapses to \(1\), which is why the ask allows \(a=1\).
